decks.title: Electromagnetic Induction — Part 1: Faraday’s law and Lenz’s law
goals: Define magnetic flux and state Faraday’s laws of electromagnetic induction
Calculate the induced emf from a changing flux
Use Lenz’s law to find the direction of an induced current, and relate it to conservation of energy

slides.heading: Electromagnetic Induction
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a changing magnetic flux produces an emf, how big it is, and which way the induced current flows.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: experiments, magnetic flux, Faraday’s law, Lenz’s law, conservation of energy

slides.narration: Almost every watt of electricity in India’s grid comes from electromagnetic induction in power-station generators. In 1831 Faraday found that a changing magnetic field can drive a current in a closed coil with no battery at all. In this part we define magnetic flux, state Faraday’s law for the size of the induced emf, and use Lenz’s law to find its direction.

slides.heading: Faraday’s experiments
slides.body_md: A coil connected to a galvanometer shows a current only while something is **changing**:
bullets: A magnet moved towards or away from the coil (faster motion, bigger deflection; reversing the motion reverses the current).
The coil moved near a stationary magnet: only relative motion matters.
The current in a nearby coil switched on or off, or varied.

rows: Magnet held still in the coil

visual.alt: Table of Faraday’s observations: no deflection with a still magnet, opposite deflections for pushing in and pulling out, brief kicks when a nearby circuit is switched

slides.narration: Faraday’s experiments all had one thing in common. A magnet resting inside a coil gives no current at all. Push its north pole in and the galvanometer kicks one way; pull it out and it kicks the other way, more strongly if you move faster. Moving the coil instead of the magnet works just as well. Switching a current on or off in a neighbouring coil also gives a brief kick. Change is what matters.

slides.heading: Magnetic flux
slides.body_md:
The **magnetic flux** through a plane area $A$ in a uniform field $B$ is
$$\Phi_B = \vec B\cdot\vec A = BA\cos\theta$$
where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec B$ and the normal to the area. SI unit: **weber** (Wb) $= 1$ T m². For $N$ turns the **flux linkage** is $N\Phi_B$.
bullets: Flux can change by changing $B$, the area $A$, or the angle $\theta$.
For a non-uniform field: $\Phi_B = \int \vec B\cdot d\vec A$.

visual.alt: Table of flux for a coil face-on, tilted and edge-on to the field

slides.narration: Magnetic flux measures how much field passes through an area: B times A times cos theta, where theta is between the field and the normal to the area. Its unit is the weber, one tesla square metre. A coil of N turns links N times this flux. The flux can be changed in three ways: change the field, change the area, or turn the coil. Each of these induces an emf.

slides.heading: Faraday’s law of induction
slides.body_md:
The magnitude of the induced emf equals the **rate of change of magnetic flux linkage**:
$$\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$
The minus sign expresses Lenz’s law (direction). The induced current is $I = \varepsilon/R$ in a circuit of resistance $R$.
bullets: A steady flux, however large, induces no emf.
Faster change, larger emf; more turns, larger emf.

visual.alt: Flux through a single loop rising steadily for 2 seconds, staying constant for 2 seconds and falling to zero in 1 second, with the induced emf: minus 5 millivolts, then zero, then plus 10 millivolts
visual.caption: The emf is minus the slope of the flux graph: steady flux gives no emf.

slides.narration: Faraday’s law says the induced emf equals the rate at which the flux linkage changes. The graph shows it clearly: while the flux rises steadily, there is a constant emf; while the flux stays the same, there is none, even though the flux is large; when the flux falls quickly, the emf is larger and opposite in sign. The minus sign in the law carries the direction, which is Lenz’s law.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a field switched off
slides.body_md: A coil of 200 turns and area 0.010 m² lies face-on in a field of 0.20 T. The field falls steadily to zero in 0.050 s. Find the induced emf.
bullets: Step 1 — change in flux per turn: $\Delta\Phi = 0.20 \times 0.010 - 0 = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb.
Step 2 — $|\varepsilon| = N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{200 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3}}{0.050} = 8.0$ V.
Step 3 — the direction is such that the induced current tries to keep the flux from falling (Lenz).

visual.alt: Flux through a single loop rising steadily for 2 seconds, staying constant for 2 seconds and falling to zero in 1 second, with the induced emf: minus 5 millivolts, then zero, then plus 10 millivolts
visual.caption: The emf is minus the slope of the flux graph: steady flux gives no emf.

slides.narration: Each turn loses a flux of B times A, two milliweber. Two hundred turns lose two hundred times that, and it all happens in one twentieth of a second, so the emf is eight volts. The induced current flows so as to oppose the decrease, trying to keep the original flux going. Doing the same change more slowly would give a smaller emf for a longer time.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: flux given as a function of time
slides.body_md: The flux through a single loop is $\Phi = (3t^2 + 2t)$ mWb, with $t$ in seconds. Find the induced emf at $t = 2$ s.
bullets: Step 1 — $\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = 6t + 2$ mWb s$^{-1}$.
Step 2 — at $t = 2$ s: $6 \times 2 + 2 = 14$ mWb s$^{-1}$.
Step 3 — $|\varepsilon| = 14$ mV (1 mWb s$^{-1}$ = 1 mV).

visual.alt: Worked table: the rate of change of flux and the emf at 0, 1 and 2 seconds: 2, 8 and 14 millivolts

slides.narration: When the flux is given as a formula, differentiate it. The rate of change is six t plus two milliweber per second, so at two seconds it is fourteen. One milliweber per second is one millivolt, so the emf is fourteen millivolts. Because the flux grows faster and faster, the emf keeps rising with time.

slides.heading: Lenz’s law
slides.body_md: The induced current flows in a direction such that its own magnetic field **opposes the change in flux** that produces it.
bullets: Inward flux increasing → induced current makes outward field (here anticlockwise).
Inward flux decreasing → induced current makes inward field (clockwise).
It opposes the **change**, not the flux itself.

slides.narration: Lenz’s law gives the direction. The induced current always flows so that its own magnetic field fights the change. Here the field into the page is growing, so the loop’s current flows anticlockwise, making a field out of the page that partly cancels the increase. If the inward field were shrinking, the current would flow clockwise to prop it up. It opposes the change, not the field.

slides.heading: Lenz’s law with a moving magnet
slides.body_md: Push the N pole of a magnet towards a coil: the near face of the coil becomes a **north** pole and **repels** the magnet. Pull it away: the near face becomes a **south** pole and **attracts** it.

slides.narration: Try it with a magnet and a coil. As the north pole approaches, the induced current makes the near face of the coil a north pole too, so the coil pushes back on the magnet. As you pull the magnet away, the near face becomes a south pole and pulls it back. Either way, you have to do work against the coil to move the magnet, and that work becomes the electrical energy of the current.

slides.heading: Lenz’s law and conservation of energy
slides.body_md: If the induced current **helped** the change instead of opposing it, the magnet would be pulled in faster, inducing a bigger current, pulling harder still — energy from nothing. Opposition means **work must be done** to keep the change going, and that work appears as electrical energy (and heat in the circuit).

rows: work is needed; energy is conserved
motion would speed up by itself: perpetual motion, impossible

visual.alt: Table contrasting an induced current that opposes the change, which conserves energy, with one that helps it, which would give perpetual motion

slides.narration: Lenz’s law is really conservation of energy. Suppose the induced current helped the motion instead. The magnet would be pulled in faster, the current would grow, and the pull would grow too: you would get ever-increasing electrical energy from nothing. Because the induced current opposes the change, you must keep doing work to move the magnet, and exactly that work becomes the energy in the circuit.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding the direction
slides.body_md: A rectangular loop lies flat on a table, seen from above, in a vertical magnetic field pointing **upwards** (towards you). The field is **decreasing**. Find the direction of the induced current as seen from above.
bullets: Step 1 — flux: upwards (towards the viewer), decreasing.
Step 2 — Lenz: the induced field must point **upwards** to oppose the decrease.
Step 3 — right-hand rule: an upward field at the centre needs an **anticlockwise** current as seen from above.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Induced current opposes the change in flux

visual.alt: Summary table of magnetic flux, Faraday’s law, ways to change flux and Lenz’s law

slides.narration: To sum up: magnetic flux is B A cos theta, measured in webers. Whenever the flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf is induced equal to the rate of change of flux linkage. A steady flux induces nothing. The direction is given by Lenz’s law: the induced current opposes the change that causes it, which is a consequence of conservation of energy.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Write the flux first, $BA\cos\theta$, with θ measured from the **normal** to the coil.
For direction questions use three steps: flux direction, increasing or decreasing, then the right-hand rule.
Say “opposes the **change** in flux”, not “opposes the flux”.
Convert cm² and mWb before substituting.

slides.narration: Start every induction problem by writing the flux, and measure the angle from the normal to the coil. For directions, go step by step: which way is the flux, is it growing or shrinking, and which current makes an opposing field. Be careful with the wording: the induced current opposes the change in flux, not the flux itself.

slides.heading: Motional emf and inductance
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the emf in a moving conductor, and how coils induce emfs in themselves and in each other.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: motional emf, rotating rod, self-inductance, mutual inductance

slides.narration: A conductor moving through a magnetic field has an emf across it, because its free charges are pushed by the magnetic force. That is the principle of every generator. In this part we derive the motional emf, look at a rotating rod, and then meet inductance: the property that makes a coil oppose changes in its own current, and lets one coil induce an emf in another.

slides.heading: Motional emf in a sliding rod
slides.body_md:
A rod of length $l$ slides with speed $v$ on rails, perpendicular to a uniform field $B$. The area of the circuit grows at rate $lv$, so
$$\varepsilon = \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = \dfrac{d(Blx)}{dt} = Blv$$
bullets: Charge picture: each free charge in the rod feels $q\vec v \times \vec B$ along the rod, which drives the current.
With resistance $R$: $I = Blv/R$.

slides.narration: A rod sliding along a pair of rails in a magnetic field makes a circuit whose area keeps growing. If the rod is a distance x from the end, the flux is B l x, so its rate of change is B l times dx by dt, which is B l v. Equivalently, every free charge in the moving rod feels a magnetic force q v cross B along the rod, and this force pumps the charges round the circuit.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: rod, current and force
slides.body_md: A rod 0.50 m long slides at 4.0 m s$^{-1}$ on rails in a field of 0.30 T; the circuit resistance is 2.0 Ω. Find the emf, the current, the force needed to keep the rod moving steadily, and the power.
bullets: Step 1 — $\varepsilon = Blv = 0.30 \times 0.50 \times 4.0 = 0.60$ V; $I = \dfrac{0.60}{2.0} = 0.30$ A.
Step 2 — magnetic force on the rod $IlB = 0.30 \times 0.50 \times 0.30 = 0.045$ N, opposing the motion, so the same push is needed.
Step 3 — mechanical power $Fv = 0.045 \times 4.0 = 0.18$ W $= I^2R = 0.18$ W.

slides.narration: The emf is B l v, zero point six volts, driving zero point three amperes through two ohms. The current in the rod feels a magnetic force I l B of zero point zero four five newton, pointing backwards, so you must push with that force to keep it moving steadily. Your mechanical power, force times speed, is zero point one eight watt, exactly the heat produced in the resistance: energy is conserved.

slides.heading: A rotating rod
slides.body_md:
A rod of length $l$ rotates with angular speed $\omega$ about one end, in a plane perpendicular to a uniform field $B$. A small element at distance $r$ moves at speed $\omega r$, so
$$\varepsilon = \int_0^l B\,\omega r\,dr = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$$
bullets: The emf is between the centre and the rim (or the ends of the rod).
A spinning metal wheel works the same way, each spoke an emf $\tfrac12 B\omega l^2$ in parallel.

visual.alt: Table of how the emf of a rotating rod changes when angular speed, length or field is doubled

slides.narration: Now spin a rod about one end in a field at right angles to its plane. Different parts of the rod move at different speeds: the end at omega l and the centre not at all. Adding up B times speed times length for each small piece gives one half B omega l squared. Note the l squared: doubling the length makes the emf four times larger.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a rotating rod
slides.body_md: A metal rod 1.0 m long rotates about one end at 20 rad s$^{-1}$ in a plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.40 T. Find the emf between its ends.
bullets: Step 1 — $\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^2 = 0.5 \times 0.40 \times 20 \times 1.0^2 = 4.0$ V.
Step 2 — the average speed of the rod is $\omega l/2 = 10$ m s$^{-1}$, so $\varepsilon = B l v_\text{avg}$ gives the same answer.

slides.heading: Self-induction
slides.body_md:
When the current in a coil changes, its own flux changes and an emf is induced in it that **opposes the change in current** (a back emf):
$$N\Phi = LI,\qquad \varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$$
$L$ is the **self-inductance**, unit **henry** (H) $= 1$ V s A$^{-1}$.

slides.narration: A coil links its own magnetic flux. If its current changes, that flux changes, so the coil induces an emf in itself, opposing the change in current. The flux linkage is proportional to the current, N phi equals L I, and the back emf is minus L d I by dt. The constant L is the self-inductance, measured in henries. Inductance acts like inertia for current.

slides.heading: Inductance of a long solenoid
slides.body_md:
For a long solenoid of $N$ turns, length $l$, cross-section $A$ ($n = N/l$), field $B = \mu_0 nI$, flux linkage $N BA$:
$$L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l} = \mu_0 n^2 A l$$
With a core of relative permeability $\mu_r$: $L = \mu_r\mu_0 n^2 A l$.
bullets: L depends only on geometry (turns, area, length) and the core, not on the current.
Energy stored: $U = \tfrac12 LI^2$ (in the magnetic field).

visual.alt: Table of how the self-inductance of a solenoid changes with turns, area and core

slides.narration: For a long solenoid, multiply the field mu nought n I by the area and the number of turns to get the flux linkage, then divide by I. The result is mu nought N squared A over l. Self-inductance depends only on how the coil is built and what is inside it: doubling the turns makes it four times larger, and an iron core multiplies it by the relative permeability. The current does not affect L.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a solenoid’s back emf
slides.body_md: An air-cored solenoid has 500 turns, length 25 cm and cross-section 4.0 cm². Find its self-inductance, and the back emf when its current rises steadily from 0 to 2.0 A in 0.010 s.
bullets: Step 1 — $L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 500^2 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-4}}{0.25} \approx 5.03 \times 10^{-4}$ H (about 0.50 mH).
Step 2 — $|\varepsilon| = L\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 5.03 \times 10^{-4} \times \dfrac{2.0}{0.010} \approx 0.10$ V.

slides.heading: Mutual induction
slides.body_md:
A changing current in one coil induces an emf in a nearby coil. The flux linked with coil 2 is proportional to the current in coil 1:
$$N_2\Phi_2 = M I_1,\qquad \varepsilon_2 = -M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}$$
$M$ is the **mutual inductance** (henry); $M_{12} = M_{21}$.

The flux linked with coil two is proportional to the current in coil one, with the constant M, the mutual inductance. The emf in coil two is minus M times the rate of change of current in coil one. slides.heading: What mutual inductance depends on
slides.body_md:
For a short solenoid (radius $r_1$, $n_1$ turns per metre) inside a long one ($n_2$ turns per metre), over a common length $l$:
$$M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 \pi r_1^2 l$$
bullets: Number of turns of both coils.
Their sizes and **separation**, and their **relative orientation** (coaxial gives the most linkage; perpendicular axes give little).
The core: an iron core multiplies M by $\mu_r$.

visual.alt: Table of mutual inductance for different arrangements of two coils

slides.narration: For one solenoid wound inside another, all the flux of the inner coil’s area links both, and M is mu nought n one n two times the inner area times the common length. In general, mutual inductance grows with the numbers of turns and the area shared, falls as the coils are moved apart or turned so that their axes are at right angles, and is multiplied greatly by a common iron core, as in a transformer.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: an emf in the secondary
slides.body_md: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.15 H. The current in the first falls steadily from 4.0 A to zero in 0.020 s. Find the emf induced in the second.
bullets: Step 1 — $\dfrac{\Delta I_1}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{4.0}{0.020} = 200$ A s$^{-1}$.
Step 2 — $|\varepsilon_2| = M\dfrac{\Delta I_1}{\Delta t} = 0.15 \times 200 = 30$ V.
Step 3 — direction: the induced current in coil 2 tries to keep the flux from falling (Lenz).

slides.narration: To sum up: a rod moving through a field has an emf B l v, and the magnetic force on the induced current opposes the motion, so the work done becomes electrical energy. Units: henry = V s A⁻¹ = Wb A⁻¹.

When asked what inductance depends on, list the geometry and the core, and say clearly that it does not depend on the current. And remember a henry is a volt second per ampere.

notes.title: Electromagnetic Induction — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Magnetic flux and Faraday’s law
sections.body_md:
**Faraday’s experiments:** a current is induced in a closed coil only while the magnetic flux through it **changes** — by moving a magnet or the coil, or by changing the current in a nearby coil. Faster change gives a larger current.

**Magnetic flux:** $\Phi_B = \vec B\cdot\vec A = BA\cos\theta$ (θ between $\vec B$ and the normal), unit weber (Wb = T m²). For a non-uniform field $\Phi_B = \int \vec B\cdot d\vec A$. Flux linkage of $N$ turns: $N\Phi_B$.

**Faraday’s law:** $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$; induced current $I = \varepsilon/R$. Flux can be changed by changing $B$, $A$ or θ. A steady flux induces nothing.

key_terms.definition_md: Φ = BA cos θ; the amount of magnetic field passing through an area, in webers.
Production of an emf in a circuit by a changing magnetic flux.

visual.alt: Flux through a single loop rising steadily for 2 seconds, staying constant for 2 seconds and falling to zero in 1 second, with the induced emf: minus 5 millivolts, then zero, then plus 10 millivolts
visual.caption: The emf is minus the slope of the flux graph: steady flux gives no emf.

sections.heading: 2. Lenz’s law
sections.body_md:
The induced current flows in such a direction that its magnetic field **opposes the change in flux** producing it (the minus sign in Faraday’s law).

**Method:** (1) direction of the flux; (2) increasing or decreasing; (3) induced field opposite to the change; (4) right-hand rule for the current.

- N pole approaching a coil → near face of the coil becomes N (repels); N pole receding → near face S (attracts).
- **Energy conservation:** because the induced current opposes the motion, work must be done to keep the flux changing; this work becomes electrical energy and heat. If it helped the change, energy would appear from nothing.

key_terms.definition_md: The induced current opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it.

sections.heading: 3. Motional emf
sections.body_md:
**Sliding rod** (length $l$, speed $v$, perpendicular to uniform $B$): flux $\Phi = Blx$, so $\varepsilon = \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = Blv$. Equivalently each free charge feels $q\vec v \times \vec B$ along the rod.

With circuit resistance $R$: $I = \dfrac{Blv}{R}$; magnetic force on the rod $F = IlB = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$, opposing the motion; power needed $Fv = \dfrac{B^2l^2v^2}{R} = I^2R$.

**Rotating rod** (length $l$, angular speed ω, about one end, perpendicular to $B$): $\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.

sections.heading: 4. Self-inductance
sections.body_md:
A changing current in a coil changes its own flux and induces a **back emf** opposing the change: $N\Phi = LI$, $\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$. Unit: henry (H = V s A⁻¹ = Wb A⁻¹).

**Long solenoid:** $L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2A}{l} = \mu_0 n^2 A l$; with a core $\mu_r\mu_0 n^2 A l$.

**Factors:** number of turns (∝ N² at fixed length), area, length, and the core’s permeability — not the current. Inductance plays the role of inertia for current. (Energy stored: $\tfrac12 LI^2$.)

key_terms.definition_md: Flux linkage per unit current in a coil, L = NΦ/I; also the back emf per unit rate of change of current.
Inductance in which a change of 1 A s⁻¹ induces 1 V.

sections.heading: 5. Mutual inductance
sections.body_md:
A changing current in coil 1 induces an emf in coil 2: $N_2\Phi_2 = MI_1$, $\varepsilon_2 = -M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}$; $M_{12} = M_{21}$.

**Coaxial solenoids** (inner radius $r_1$, turns per metre $n_1$, $n_2$, common length $l$): $M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 \pi r_1^2 l$.

**Factors:** numbers of turns, areas, separation, relative orientation (coaxial: large; axes perpendicular: very small), and a common core ($\times\mu_r$). Used in transformers and induction chargers.

key_terms.definition_md: Flux linked with one coil per unit current in the other, M = N₂Φ₂/I₁.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A coil held at rest in a very strong but steady magnetic field has a large induced emf.
questions.solution_md: False. The induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux. A steady flux, however large, induces no emf.

questions.stem_md: A coil of 100 turns, each of area 50 cm², lies face-on in a magnetic field that increases steadily at 0.20 T s⁻¹. Find the induced emf, in volts.
questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon = NA\dfrac{dB}{dt} = 100 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.20 = 0.10$ V.

questions.stem_md: A flat coil of area 0.020 m² is in a uniform field of 0.50 T. The normal to the coil makes 60° with the field. The flux through one turn is
questions.solution_md: $\Phi = BA\cos 60^\circ = 0.50 \times 0.020 \times 0.5 = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A coil of 50 turns and area 0.040 m² is turned in 0.10 s from facing a uniform 0.25 T field (plane perpendicular to B) to lying edge-on to it (plane parallel to B). Find the average induced emf, in volts.
questions.solution_md: Flux per turn changes from $BA = 0.25 \times 0.040 = 0.010$ Wb to 0. $|\varepsilon| = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{50 \times 0.010}{0.10} = 5.0$ V.

questions.stem_md: A flexible single loop lies face-on in a uniform field of 0.50 T. It is squeezed so that its area falls from 100 cm² to 40 cm² in 0.20 s. Find the average induced emf, in millivolts.
questions.solution_md: $\Delta A = (100 - 40) \times 10^{-4} = 6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m². $|\varepsilon| = \dfrac{B\Delta A}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{0.50 \times 6.0 \times 10^{-3}}{0.20} = 0.015$ V, i.e. $0.015 \times 1000 = 15$ mV.

marking_scheme.step: ΔA in m² and ε = BΔA/Δt

questions.stem_md: The flux through a single loop varies as $\Phi = (5t^2 - 4t + 1)$ mWb, with $t$ in seconds. The magnitude of the induced emf at $t = 1$ s is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = 10t - 4 = 6$ mWb s$^{-1}$ at $t = 1$ s, so $|\varepsilon| = 6$ mV — option (b).

questions.stem_md: On a graph of magnetic flux through a coil against time, the induced emf is largest where the graph
questions.solution_md: The emf is the rate of change of flux, the slope of the graph — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A coil’s number of turns is doubled, and the same change of field is made in half the time. The induced emf becomes
questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon = N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$: doubling N doubles it; halving Δt doubles it again — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A coil of 100 turns and total resistance 5.0 Ω is in a circuit. The flux through each turn changes by 2.0 × 10⁻³ Wb. Find the total charge that flows, in millicoulombs.
questions.solution_md: $q = I\Delta t = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}\Delta t = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R} = \dfrac{100 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3}}{5.0} = 0.040$ C, i.e. $0.040 \times 1000 = 40$ mC (whatever the speed of the change).

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of magnetic flux is the ___.
questions.solution_md: The **weber** (Wb), equal to one tesla square metre.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Moving a magnet faster into a coil gives a larger deflection of a galvanometer connected to the coil.

**Reason (R):** The induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; faster motion changes the flux faster, which by Faraday’s law gives a larger emf and current — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a ballistic galvanometer, first slowly and then quickly. Explain why the total charge that flows is the same both times, although the current is not.

answer.model_answer_md: The emf is $N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$, so a faster push gives a **larger current** for a **shorter time**. The charge is $q = I\Delta t = N\Delta\Phi/R$, which depends only on the **total change of flux** and the resistance, the same in both pushes.

questions.solution_md: q = NΔΦ/R is independent of Δt.

questions.stem_md: The north pole of a bar magnet is pulled AWAY from one face of a coil. The induced current makes that face of the coil

options.text_md: a north pole, which repels the magnet
a north pole, which attracts the magnet
a south pole, which attracts the magnet

questions.solution_md: The induced current opposes the change (the magnet moving away), so the near face attracts it: it becomes a south pole — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet is dropped vertically through a horizontal closed copper ring. While it approaches and passes through the ring, its acceleration is
questions.solution_md: The induced current in the ring opposes the relative motion: it repels the magnet as it approaches and attracts it as it leaves, so the magnet always feels an upward force — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A horizontal loop lies on a table, seen from above. A magnetic field points vertically DOWN through it and is INCREASING. Seen from above, the induced current is
questions.solution_md: Downward flux is increasing, so the induced field must point up; an upward field at the centre needs an anticlockwise current seen from above — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two coaxial loops face each other. A current is suddenly switched on in loop 1. While the current is growing, the current induced in loop 2 is

options.text_md: in the same sense as in loop 1, so the loops attract
opposite in sense to that in loop 1, so the loops repel
opposite in sense, so the loops attract
zero, because loop 2 has no battery

questions.solution_md: Loop 2 opposes the growing flux from loop 1, so its current circulates the other way; antiparallel currents repel — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lenz’s law is consistent with the law of conservation of energy.

**Reason (R):** Because the induced current opposes the change producing it, work must be done to keep the flux changing, and that work appears as electrical energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; R is exactly why Lenz’s law agrees with energy conservation — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? According to Lenz’s law, the induced current always produces a field opposite to the existing magnetic field.
questions.solution_md: False. It opposes the CHANGE in flux. If the flux is decreasing, the induced field is in the same direction as the existing field.

questions.stem_md: A long straight wire carries a steady current upwards in the plane of the page. A rectangular loop lies in the page to the right of the wire and is moved further to the right. Seen from the front, the current induced in the loop is

options.text_md: zero, because the current in the wire is steady
clockwise only while it is close to the wire

questions.solution_md: To the right of an upward current, the field points into the page. Moving away, this inward flux decreases, so the induced current makes an inward field to oppose the decrease: clockwise — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A magnet falls through a vertical copper tube that is closed into a ring at the top, and through a similar ring that has a narrow cut in it. Through which ring does it fall more slowly? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Through the **closed** ring. There the changing flux drives an induced **current** whose field opposes the magnet’s motion (Lenz), slowing it. In the **cut** ring an emf is induced but **no current** can flow, so there is no opposing force and the magnet falls freely.

questions.solution_md: Induced current needs a closed path.

marking_scheme.step: Closed ring: induced current opposes motion
Cut ring: no current, no opposing force

questions.stem_md: Explain how Lenz’s law follows from the conservation of energy.

answer.model_answer_md: Suppose the induced current **helped** the change, e.g. attracted an approaching magnet. The magnet would speed up, the current would grow and pull harder: electrical and kinetic energy would increase with no work done — impossible. So the current must **oppose** the change; then **work must be done** to move the magnet, and this work becomes the electrical energy.

questions.solution_md: Consider what would happen if the current aided the change.

marking_scheme.step: Helping current would create energy from nothing
Opposition means work is done, which becomes electrical energy

questions.stem_md: A square loop lies in the plane of the page, in a uniform magnetic field directed out of the page. State the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise, seen from the front) of the induced current when (a) the field is increasing, (b) the field is decreasing, (c) the loop is rotated about one side so that its plane turns away from facing the field.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Outward flux increasing → induced field **into** the page → **clockwise**.
(b) Outward flux decreasing → induced field **out of** the page → **anticlockwise**.
(c) Turning the loop reduces the outward flux (Φ = BA cos θ falls) → induced field out of the page → **anticlockwise** (at least while the loop still faces mainly outward).

questions.solution_md: Flux direction, increase or decrease, opposing field, right-hand rule.

questions.stem_md: A metal rod 20 cm long moves at 5.0 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to its length and to a uniform field of 0.50 T. Find the emf between its ends, in volts.
questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon = Blv = 0.50 \times 0.20 \times 5.0 = 0.5$ V.

questions.stem_md: An aircraft with a wingspan of 30 m flies horizontally at 250 m s⁻¹ through a region where the vertical component of the magnetic field is 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T. The emf between its wing tips is about
questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon = Blv = 4.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 30 \times 250 = 0.3$ V; only the vertical component is cut by the horizontal wings — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A rod slides on rails in a uniform field and is kept moving at constant speed by an external force. The speed is doubled. The external force needed and the power supplied become

options.text_md: the same and twice as large
four times and eight times as large
twice and four times as large

questions.solution_md: $F = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R} \propto v$ and $P = Fv \propto v^2$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A copper rod 0.50 m long rotates about one end at 40 rad s⁻¹ in a plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.20 T. Find the emf between its ends, in volts.
questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^2 = 0.5 \times 0.20 \times 40 \times 0.50^2 = 1$ V.

questions.stem_md: A metal wheel with 10 spokes, each of length $l$, rotates with angular speed $\omega$ in a plane perpendicular to a uniform field $B$. The emf between the axle and the rim is
questions.solution_md: Every spoke has the same emf $\tfrac12 B\omega l^2$ between axle and rim, and the spokes are in parallel, so the emf is that of one spoke — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A straight rod moves through a uniform magnetic field with its velocity parallel to the field. The emf between its ends is
questions.solution_md: With $\vec v \parallel \vec B$, $q\vec v \times \vec B = 0$: the rod cuts no field lines — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A straight conductor moving through a uniform magnetic field always has an emf induced across its ends.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic force on a moving charge is $q\vec v \times \vec B$.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: if the conductor moves parallel to the field, or along its own length, $\vec v \times \vec B$ has no component along the rod and there is no emf — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A horizontal rod of mass 20 g and length 20 cm slides without friction down a pair of vertical rails joined at the top through a 1.0 Ω resistor, in a horizontal field of 0.50 T perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Explain why it reaches a constant (terminal) speed and find that speed. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

answer.model_answer_md:
As the rod falls, the emf $Blv$ drives a current $I = Blv/R$, and the force $IlB = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$ acts **upwards**, opposing the fall (Lenz). It grows with speed until it equals the weight; then the net force is zero and the speed stays constant.
$mg = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$ gives $v = \dfrac{mgR}{B^2l^2} = \dfrac{0.020 \times 9.8 \times 1.0}{0.50^2 \times 0.20^2} = 19.6$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Balance the magnetic force B²l²v/R against mg.

questions.stem_md: A square loop of side 10 cm moves at a steady 5.0 cm s⁻¹ into, through and out of a region of uniform field 0.40 T that is wider than the loop, with the field perpendicular to the loop. Describe the emf while the loop (a) enters, (b) is wholly inside, (c) leaves the field, and find its size in (a).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Entering:** the flux grows steadily, so there is a constant emf $Bav = 0.40 \times 0.10 \times 0.050 = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ V.
(b) **Wholly inside:** the flux is constant, so the emf is **zero**.
(c) **Leaving:** the flux falls steadily, so there is an emf of the **same size but opposite sign** (the current flows the other way).

questions.solution_md: Track the flux; emf is its rate of change.

questions.stem_md: The number of turns of a long solenoid is doubled, keeping its length and cross-section the same. Its self-inductance becomes
questions.solution_md: $L = \mu_0 N^2 A/l \propto N^2$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of self-inductance and of mutual inductance is the ___.
questions.solution_md: The **henry** (H), equal to one volt second per ampere.

questions.stem_md: The current in a coil of self-inductance 0.40 H falls steadily from 5.0 A to zero in 0.10 s. Find the magnitude of the induced emf, in volts.
questions.solution_md: $|\varepsilon| = L\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 0.40 \times \dfrac{5.0}{0.10} = 20$ V.

questions.stem_md: An air-cored solenoid has 1000 turns, length 50 cm and cross-sectional area 10 cm². Find its self-inductance, in millihenry (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1000^2 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3}}{0.50} \approx 2.51 \times 10^{-3}$ H. In mH: $2.51 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{3} = 2.51$.

questions.stem_md: A soft-iron core of relative permeability 1000 is slid fully into an air-cored solenoid. Its self-inductance

options.text_md: is unchanged, because L depends only on turns and size

questions.solution_md: With a core, $L = \mu_r\mu_0 n^2 A l$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The steady current through a coil is doubled. Its self-inductance
questions.solution_md: Flux linkage doubles with the current, so $L = N\Phi/I$ is unchanged; L depends on geometry and core only — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.20 H. The current in the first coil rises steadily from 0 to 3.0 A in 0.050 s. Find the emf induced in the second coil, in volts.
questions.solution_md: $|\varepsilon_2| = M\dfrac{\Delta I_1}{\Delta t} = 0.20 \times \dfrac{3.0}{0.050} = 12$ V.

questions.stem_md: A short solenoid of radius 1.0 cm with 1000 turns per metre lies coaxially inside a long solenoid with 2000 turns per metre; the common length is 50 cm. Find their mutual inductance, in millihenry (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 \pi r_1^2 l = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1000 \times 2000 \times \pi \times 0.010^2 \times 0.50 \approx 3.95 \times 10^{-4}$ H. In mH: $3.95 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{3} = 0.395$.

questions.stem_md: Two coils on a circuit board must interfere with each other as little as possible. They should be placed

options.text_md: with their axes at right angles to each other
side by side with parallel axes

questions.solution_md: With perpendicular axes, very little of one coil’s flux threads the other, so M is very small — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A steady current in one coil induces no emf in a nearby coil.

**Reason (R):** The emf induced in the second coil is proportional to the rate of change of current in the first.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; with a steady current $dI_1/dt = 0$, so $\varepsilon_2 = -M\,dI_1/dt = 0$, which explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Inserting a soft-iron core into a coil increases its self-inductance.

**Reason (R):** Iron is a diamagnetic material.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: iron is ferromagnetic, with a very large μr, which is why L increases — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The self-inductance of a coil increases when the current through it increases.

**Reason (R):** The flux linked with a coil is proportional to the current through it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: because the flux linkage is proportional to the current, their ratio L is constant — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An inductor of 0.20 H carries a steady current of 3.0 A. The energy stored in its magnetic field is
questions.solution_md: $U = \tfrac{1}{2}LI^2 = 0.5 \times 0.20 \times 3.0^2 = 0.9$ J — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Match each change in Column A with its effect on the mutual inductance of two coils in Column B.

options.text_md: One coil turned so the axes are perpendicular

questions.solution_md: Apart → decreases (1 → q); iron core → increases greatly (2 → s); perpendicular → very small (3 → p); current doubled → unchanged (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: Self-inductance is sometimes called “electrical inertia”. Explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: Mass resists **changes in velocity**; a coil’s self-inductance resists **changes in current**. When the current tries to change, the back emf $-L\,dI/dt$ opposes the change, so the current cannot rise or fall instantly. A larger L, like a larger mass, means a stronger opposition to change.

questions.solution_md: Compare L dI/dt with m dv/dt.

marking_scheme.step: Opposes change in current as mass opposes change in velocity
Back emf −L dI/dt; larger L, more opposition

questions.stem_md: State four factors on which the mutual inductance of a pair of coils depends.

answer.model_answer_md: The **numbers of turns** of the two coils; their **cross-sectional areas** (sizes); their **separation**; their **relative orientation** (coaxial or not); and the **medium/core** between them (an iron core increases M greatly). It does not depend on the currents.

questions.solution_md: Geometry, arrangement and core.

questions.stem_md: When a switch is opened in a circuit containing a large electromagnet, a spark often jumps across the switch contacts. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Opening the switch makes the current fall to zero **very quickly**, so $dI/dt$ is very large. The coil’s large self-inductance then induces a **large back emf** ($L\,dI/dt$) that tries to keep the current flowing; this high voltage across the opening gap **ionises the air** and a spark jumps.

questions.solution_md: Large L and large dI/dt give a large emf.

marking_scheme.step: Rapid fall in current: large dI/dt
Large induced emf ionises the air: spark

questions.stem_md: Derive an expression for the self-inductance of a long air-cored solenoid of $N$ turns, length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$.

answer.model_answer_md:
With current $I$, the field inside is uniform: $B = \mu_0 nI = \mu_0\dfrac{N}{l}I$. The flux through each turn is $BA$, so the total flux linkage is $N\Phi = N\mu_0\dfrac{N}{l}IA$. Since $N\Phi = LI$:
$$L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l} = \mu_0 n^2 A l.$$
It depends only on the turns, area and length (and on $\mu_r$ if there is a core).

questions.solution_md: Flux linkage divided by current.

questions.stem_md: (a) State Faraday’s laws of electromagnetic induction and Lenz’s law. (b) Explain how Lenz’s law is a consequence of conservation of energy. (c) A coil of 300 turns and area 0.020 m², with resistance 12 Ω, lies face-on in a field of 0.60 T. The field is reduced steadily to zero in 0.15 s. Find the induced emf and current.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Faraday:** an emf is induced in a circuit whenever the magnetic flux linked with it changes; its magnitude equals the rate of change of flux linkage, $\varepsilon = -N\,d\Phi/dt$. **Lenz:** the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in flux producing it.

(b) If the induced current aided the change (e.g. attracted an approaching magnet), the magnet would accelerate and the current would grow without any work being done — energy from nothing. Because the current opposes the change, work must be done against it, and this work is converted into electrical energy and heat.

(c) $|\varepsilon| = \dfrac{NA\Delta B}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{300 \times 0.020 \times 0.60}{0.15} = 24$ V; $I = \dfrac{24}{12} = 2.0$ A, flowing so as to oppose the decrease in flux.

questions.solution_md: State the laws; argue from energy; then ε = NAΔB/Δt and I = ε/R.

questions.stem_md: (a) A rod of length $l$ slides with speed $v$ along a pair of parallel rails in a uniform field $B$ perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Derive the emf induced in the rod. (b) Show that the magnetic force on the rod opposes its motion, and that the mechanical power needed equals the electrical power dissipated. (c) Find the emf, current and force for $B = 0.60$ T, $l = 25$ cm, $v = 2.0$ m s$^{-1}$ and circuit resistance 0.50 Ω.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) If the rod is a distance $x$ from the closed end, the flux through the circuit is $\Phi = Blx$. As the rod moves, $dx/dt = v$, so $\varepsilon = \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = Blv$ (in magnitude).

(b) The current is $I = Blv/R$. The rod carrying it in field $B$ feels $F = IlB = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$, directed **against** $\vec v$ (by Lenz’s law, and by $I\vec l \times \vec B$). To keep $v$ constant an equal external force is needed; its power is $Fv = \dfrac{B^2l^2v^2}{R} = I^2R$, the power dissipated in the resistance: energy is conserved.

(c) $\varepsilon = 0.60 \times 0.25 \times 2.0 = 0.30$ V; $I = \dfrac{0.30}{0.50} = 0.60$ A; $F = IlB = 0.60 \times 0.25 \times 0.60 = 0.090$ N.

questions.solution_md: Φ = Blx → Blv; F = IlB opposes v; P = Fv = I²R.

questions.stem_md: (a) A metal rod of length $l$ rotates with angular speed $\omega$ about one end, in a plane perpendicular to a uniform field $B$. Derive the emf between its ends. (b) Find the emf for $B = 0.50$ T, $\omega = 30$ rad s$^{-1}$ and $l = 40$ cm. (c) If the rod’s ends are connected through a 2.0 Ω resistor using a sliding contact, find the current and the power needed to keep it rotating (neglect friction and the rod’s resistance).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An element $dr$ at distance $r$ from the axis moves with speed $\omega r$ perpendicular to $B$, so it contributes $d\varepsilon = B\omega r\,dr$. Adding from $0$ to $l$: $\varepsilon = \int_0^l B\omega r\,dr = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$.

(b) $\varepsilon = 0.5 \times 0.50 \times 30 \times 0.40^2 = 1.2$ V.

(c) $I = \dfrac{1.2}{2.0} = 0.60$ A; power $= \varepsilon I = 1.2 \times 0.60 = 0.72$ W, supplied by whatever keeps the rod turning (the induced current’s force opposes the rotation).

questions.solution_md: Integrate Bωr dr; then Ohm’s law and P = εI.

questions.stem_md: (a) Define mutual inductance. (b) Derive an expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids of the same length $l$, the inner of radius $r_1$ with $n_1$ turns per unit length and the outer with $n_2$ turns per unit length. (c) Find M for $n_1 = 1500$ m⁻¹, $n_2 = 800$ m⁻¹, $r_1 = 2.0$ cm, $l = 40$ cm, and the emf induced in the inner solenoid when the current in the outer one changes at 200 A s⁻¹.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The mutual inductance M of two coils is the flux linked with one per unit current in the other: $N_1\Phi_1 = MI_2$; equivalently the emf induced in one per unit rate of change of current in the other, $\varepsilon_1 = -M\,dI_2/dt$.

(b) A current $I_2$ in the outer solenoid gives a uniform field $B_2 = \mu_0 n_2 I_2$ inside it. The inner solenoid has $n_1 l$ turns, each of area $\pi r_1^2$, so its flux linkage is $N_1\Phi_1 = (n_1 l)(\pi r_1^2)(\mu_0 n_2 I_2)$. Hence $M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 \pi r_1^2 l$ (and $M_{12} = M_{21}$).

(c) $M = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1500 \times 800 \times \pi \times 0.020^2 \times 0.40 \approx 7.58 \times 10^{-4}$ H; $|\varepsilon_1| = M \times 200 \approx 0.152$ V.

questions.solution_md: Field of the outer solenoid times the area and turns of the inner one, per unit current.

marking_scheme.step: Flux linkage of inner coil and M = μ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l

questions.stem_md: (a) What is self-induction? Define self-inductance and its SI unit. (b) State three factors on which the self-inductance of a coil depends. (c) An electromagnet has self-inductance 0.60 H and carries 4.0 A. When the circuit is broken, the current falls to zero in 2.0 ms. Find the average induced emf and the energy that was stored in the coil, and explain why a spark may appear at the switch.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Self-induction:** when the current in a coil changes, the changing flux through the coil itself induces an emf in it that opposes the change. **Self-inductance** $L$ is the flux linkage per unit current, $N\Phi = LI$, or the induced emf per unit rate of change of current, $\varepsilon = -L\,dI/dt$. Unit: **henry** (1 H = 1 V s A$^{-1}$).

(b) The number of turns (L ∝ N² for a fixed length), the area of cross-section, the length of the coil, and the permeability of the core.

(c) $|\varepsilon| = L\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{0.60 \times 4.0}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1200$ V. Energy stored $U = \tfrac{1}{2}LI^2 = 0.5 \times 0.60 \times 4.0^2 = 4.8$ J. The very large emf (about 1200 V) appears across the opening switch gap, ionising the air, and the stored energy is released in the spark.

questions.solution_md: ε = L ΔI/Δt; U = ½LI².

marking_scheme.step: Self-induction and definition of L, unit

questions.passage_md: In a school laboratory in Guwahati, a bar magnet is dropped from rest, north pole first, through a vertical coil connected to a data logger. The logger shows a short pulse of emf as the magnet enters the coil, then a second, taller and narrower pulse of the opposite sign as it leaves.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) The flux through the coil increases as the magnet enters and decreases as it leaves

**(b)** (d) The magnet is moving faster as it leaves, so the flux changes faster over a shorter time

**(c)** (i) With a closed circuit an induced **current** flows. By Lenz’s law its field **opposes** the motion: the coil repels the magnet as it enters and attracts it as it leaves, so there is an upward force and the magnet falls with acceleration **less than g**. Some of its energy becomes heat in the resistor.

**OR** (ii) The area under an emf–time pulse is $\int \varepsilon\,dt = N\Delta\Phi$, the total change of flux linkage. The flux rises by the same amount as the magnet enters as it falls when the magnet leaves, so the two areas are **equal in size** (and opposite in sign), however fast each change is.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Entering: increasing flux; leaving: decreasing flux, so the induced emf reverses — option (c).

**(b)** The magnet accelerates while falling, so the second change of flux happens faster: larger emf for a shorter time — option (d).

**(c)** (i) Opposing force from the induced current.

(ii) ∫ε dt = NΔΦ.

questions.stem_md: A length of wire is bent into a single circular loop and placed face-on in a magnetic field that is increasing steadily. The same wire is then bent into a two-turn circular coil and placed in the same way. The emf in the two-turn coil, compared with the single loop, is
questions.solution_md: With two turns the radius halves, so each turn has a quarter of the area. Flux linkage $\propto N A = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ of the single loop’s, so the emf is halved — option (a).

questions.solution_md: The flux per turn changes from $+BA$ to $-BA$, a change of $2BA$, so $|\varepsilon| = 2NBA/t$ — option (c).

clockwise, making that face a north pole

options.text_md: is pulled down onto the solenoid

questions.stem_md: A rod 40 cm long slides on rails in a uniform field of 0.50 T perpendicular to the rails; the circuit resistance is 0.80 Ω. At what speed must the rod move for a current of 0.25 A to flow? Answer in m s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Required emf $\varepsilon = IR = 0.25 \times 0.80 = 0.2$ V. Then $v = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{Bl} = \dfrac{0.2}{0.50 \times 0.40} = 1$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: A rod 30 cm long is pulled at a steady 5.0 m s⁻¹ along rails in a perpendicular field of 0.40 T; the circuit resistance is 1.2 Ω. Find the pulling force needed, in newtons.
questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon = Blv = 0.40 \times 0.30 \times 5.0 = 0.6$ V; $I = \dfrac{0.6}{1.2} = 0.5$ A; $F = IlB = 0.5 \times 0.30 \times 0.40 = 0.06$ N (equal to the opposing magnetic force).

questions.stem_md: An emf of 6.0 V is induced in a coil when the current through it rises steadily from 2.0 A to 5.0 A in 0.10 s. Find the self-inductance of the coil, in henry.
questions.solution_md: $L = \dfrac{|\varepsilon|}{\Delta I/\Delta t} = \dfrac{6.0}{3.0/0.10} = \dfrac{6.0}{30} = 0.2$ H.

questions.solution_md: $N\Phi = LI$, so $\Phi = \dfrac{LI}{N} = \dfrac{0.50 \times 2.0}{200} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb — option (d).
